We introduce a novel photometric redshift algorithm, which utilizes compelled photometry data spanning from 0.36 to 4.5 microns to derive photometric redshifts for galaxies. This compelled data is generated by applying a spectral energy distribution (SED) model to each galaxy's observed photometry, thereby accounting for the degeneracy inherent in SED fitting. The algorithm was tested on a sample of 1,000 galaxies from the CDFS and ELAIS-S1 fields, achieving a median scatter of 0.023 and a mean absolute magnitude of 0.017. The method's performance was further validated against the GOODS-N field, yielding a median scatter of 0.024 and a mean absolute magnitude of 0.020. Additionally, we demonstrate that the algorithm's accuracy is contingent upon the quality of the input data.

A Bayesian Choice Support System (BCSS) has been developed and applied to address the intricate challenge of energy system planning. This system integrates diverse data sources, including socio-economic indicators and climate projections, to identify optimal energy system configurations. The BCSS framework employs a hierarchical Bayesian approach to quantify uncertainty and supports decision-making through interactive visualizations. The study demonstrates the application of this BCSS using a case study focused on the electricity sector in the Netherlands.

We demonstrate that two-electron wavefunctions, which are antisymmetric under exchange, can always be represented as matrix product states (MPS) with a tensor bond rank of Three. This result is derived from the wavefunction's factorization along any single coordinate line. We further establish that the wavefunction's separability along a specific axis dictates the structure of the MPS representation. MPS with this rank Three constraint are known to be fully characterized by a single continuous parameter function defined over three variables. This finding is significant for the efficient compression of two-electron wavefunctions within the configuration interaction (CI) approach.

We introduce a minimal non-Abelian dark sector featuring a dark fermion coupled to an $SU(2)_D$ gauge boson, with leptonic interactions mediated by a new portal. This model offers a natural explanation for dark matter's non-baryonic composition via a novel mechanism of baryon number violation. We demonstrate that the model can simultaneously account for dark matter's relic density and the muon's anomalous magnetic moment, while remaining consistent with current experimental constraints.

The Digital Twin Earth (DTE) framework is a data-driven, real-time simulation system designed to model the Earth's physical dynamics. This approach leverages the inherent inductive biases of physics to create surrogate models that are both computationally efficient and highly accurate. This paper details the application of neural operators to develop a surrogate model for coastal flooding, a critical component of the DTE. The model is built upon the Saint-Venant equations, a set of partial differential equations that govern fluid flow. The authors describe the neural operator's training methodology, validation, and deployment within the DTE architecture. The resulting model delivers flood predictions in milliseconds, a significant improvement over traditional physics-based models that require minutes. The study concludes by outlining potential future extensions of this model.

The BeyondPlanck and Cosmoglobe collaborations are dedicated to analyzing the full Planck data set, with a primary focus on cosmic microwave background polarization. This paper details our open-access data infrastructure, detailing the tools, software, and datasets we have developed to support the scientific community. We examine our strategies for ensuring data replicability and the sustainable preservation of resources. Additionally, we outline the specific challenges and opportunities presented by incorporating third-party data into our analysis framework.

This study examines Turing patterns within networked reaction-diffusion systems, specifically focusing on the transmission of the reaction-diffusion process between nodes. We demonstrate that a diffusion process with finite transmission probability significantly influences pattern formation. Specifically, this process can either suppress or enhance Turing patterns, contingent on the system's parameters. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the pattern dynamics are governed by the interplay between the network's topology and the reaction-diffusion network's parameters.

We present a novel nonperturbative approach to the Yang-Mills theory of SU(2) gauge fields, which relies on a novel nonlocal action. This framework employs a quasiclassical approximation to derive a set of coupled, nonlinear, nonlinear differential equations for the Yang-Mills fields. These equations are solved using the numerical method, and the study analyzes the spatial and temporal evolution of the fields.

We present a theoretical investigation into the polarization characteristics of single GaN nanowires, utilizing a model that accounts for both quantum confinement and spin-orbit coupling. Our findings indicate that the polarization of these GaN nanowires is significantly more complex than that of bulk zincblende GaN. Specifically, the polarization variance varies with temperature, and this effect is markedly stronger in nanowires compared to bulk zincblende GaN.

Adversary modeling is fundamental to dialogue systems, yet it remains difficult to apply in practical scenarios because of the challenge of acquiring high-quality, labeled interaction data. This paper introduces a method to enhance adversary modeling in negotiation by leveraging the principle that similar negotiators exhibit comparable behaviors. We introduce a new metric designed to gauge the behavioral similarity between negotiators, which facilitates the identification of analogous counterparts from a vast pool of candidates. We then propose a technique for adapting data from these similar negotiators to augment the training set for a specific target negotiator. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach significantly improves performance in negotiation dialogues, with gains of up to 10.5% in the number of turns achieved and 6.8% in the total utility secured.

This study examines a light-like portion of compactification within a two-dimensional spacetime featuring a single non-compact dimension, where the compactification scale evolves dynamically according to the string tension. We demonstrate that the string tension behaves as a conformal primary field of weight $1/2$ and that its renormalized expectation value remains finite. Furthermore, we analyze the model's behavior in the infrared regime, where the string tension stabilizes to a constant value, and address the specific challenges associated with compactifications governed by light-like directions.

Balancing is a fundamental concept in the design of experiments, serving as a primary method for enhancing experimental efficiency. This paper investigates the balancing problem within a sequential experimental framework, where researchers must assign one of two treatments to each subject in an online manner. The objective is to minimize the imbalance between treatment groups, measured by the absolute difference in the counts of subjects receiving each. We introduce the Pigeonhole Design (PHD), a new assignment strategy that achieves balance in linear time. Theoretically, we demonstrate that the imbalance count generated by PHD is bounded by the square root of the total number of subjects. Furthermore, we analyze PHD from the viewpoint of online matching theory, proving that it performs at least as well as the optimal offline assignment. We also show that the design is asymptotically optimal, meaning it achieves the theoretical lower bound for the imbalance count. We further present a generalization of PHD, the Weighted Pigeonhole Design (WPHD), which maintains computational linearity while delivering superior balancing results. We also provide a theoretical lower bound for imbalance counts in online settings and demonstrate that the WPHD design meets this lower bound. Finally, we present a simulation study comparing PHD and WPHD against established designs such as Randomization and a Min-Min algorithm, showing that the new methods significantly outperform these benchmarks.

The Si/Al2O3 interface is fundamental to the creation of Si-based CMOS devices, yet its specific nature remains debated. This study utilizes first-principles calculations to examine the interfacial structure and bonding characteristics of Si(001) terminated with a monolayer of Al2O3. The findings indicate that the interface is predominantly covalent, a conclusion supported by the absence of charge transfer and minimal ionic character. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the interfacial Si atoms adopt a buckled configuration, whereas Al2O3 forms a stable, planar structure. These results demonstrate that the interfacial properties are governed by the termination type of the Al2O3 slab, thereby offering new insights into the nature of this critical interface.

This study investigates the nonlinear statistical models of the $N$-body problem, specifically focusing on the $N$-body gravitational collapse. We demonstrate that for any $N$, there exist multiple distinct initial configurations leading to black hole formation. Furthermore, we establish that the gravitational collapse initiated by these configurations occurs within a finite time duration.

This study introduces a comprehensive historical dataset on the global container shipping industry spanning from 1966 to the present. The collection includes time-series data for freight rates, shipping volume, newbuildings, second-hand transactions, and scrap prices. The data has been rigorously cleaned and validated through multiple methods, with a specific focus on addressing the scarcity of historical records. The newly compiled series are compared against existing published data to confirm their accuracy. The primary motivation behind this project is to facilitate research into the cyclical dynamics of freight rates and how they interact with newbuilding orders, second-hand market activity, and scrap prices. The resulting dataset is publicly accessible via a dedicated website.

This study examines the online anomaly detection (OAD) challenge, which involves identifying irregularities in data streams that evolve over time. OAD is essential for numerous practical applications, including intrusion detection, network monitoring, and system fault diagnosis. We present a comprehensive review of existing OAD methods, categorizing them into three distinct groups based on their operational principles: distance-based, density-based, and clustering-based techniques. Our review covers the theoretical underpinnings of these approaches, evaluates their performance, and discusses their pros and cons. Additionally, we introduce a novel meta-OAD framework that integrates various OAD methods to leverage their collective strengths. Our findings indicate that this meta-framework outperforms individual standalone detectors. The study concludes with a discussion on unresolved challenges and future research directions.

This study presents a new approach for segmenting gliomas in brain MRI images by integrating a convolutional neural network (CNN) with specific post-processing techniques. The methodology utilizes a U-Net architecture enhanced with residual connections, trained on the BRATS 2018 dataset. We evaluated the network's performance using the Dice coefficient, Jaccard index, and mean absolute error. To refine the model's raw outputs, we applied several post-processing strategies, including a simple majority vote, a modified majority vote, a median filter, and a 3D conditional random field (CRF). Comparative analysis of these post-processing methods demonstrates that the modified majority vote yields the highest accuracy. Furthermore, we examined the impact of varying the number of CTNs layers on both accuracy and computational cost. Our findings indicate that utilizing 16 convolutional layers offers the optimal balance between processing time and segmentation quality.

Triplons represent the fundamental magnetic excitations in systems with antiferromagnetic Heisenberg interactions. This study examines the microscopic mechanisms for generating triplons in quantum magnetic solids, focusing on the triplet state's energy and momentum distribution. We demonstrate that triplons can arise from the combined action of microwave fields and static fields, or from the interaction between light and matter. Furthermore, we explore the potential for generating substantial triplon populations at room temperature, which could enable the development of novel devices for information processing.

This paper introduces novel methods for defining limits and convergence within networks, extending well-established notions such as statistical, fast, and normal convergence. By employing directed sets, our approach establishes a unified framework for these concepts, thereby generalizing their traditional definitions found in literature.

This study examines the discontinuous Galerkin finite element method for solving the 1D Rosenau equation, which is a nonlinear partial differential equation. The authors introduce a novel numerical approach to address this equation, providing a theoretical proof of the stability and convergence of the resulting scheme. Numerical experiments are also presented to validate the method's accuracy and to illustrate its implementation.

This study examines the well-posedness of a semilinear parabolic-elliptic coupled partial differential equation (PDE) system. The model describes the interaction between a compressible fluid governed by the barotropic Euler equations and an incompressible fluid modeled by the Stokes equations. We establish that the resulting PDE system constitutes an infinite-dimensional saddle-point system characterized by infinite degrees of freedom. Leveraging this characterization, we apply a novel approach to prove the well-posedness of the coupled system. This method involves demonstrating the existence of a suitable saddle point inf–sup constant, thereby ensuring the well-posedness of the associated operator semigroup.

We present a theoretical investigation into the formation of Wigner excitons in van der Waals bilayers, where magnetic fields induce the crystallization of charged interlayer excitations. Our analysis reveals that these Wigner exciton crystals (WExCs) exhibit a triangular lattice structure, with their phase boundaries shifting toward lower charge densities as the magnetic field strength increases. Notably, the magnetic field significantly alters the interlayer exciton's wave function, resulting in a marked rise in the Coulomb interaction energy. This enhancement stems from the field's ability to suppress the separation between the electron and hole components of the exciton. Furthermore, we observe that the magnetic field induces a transition in the WExC lattice from a hexagonal to a square configuration.

This study introduces a method for adjusting radial velocities (RVs) derived from LAMOST medium-resolution stellar spectra. The approach involves dividing the spectral line region into two distinct parts: the blue-shifted and red-shifted wings. By fitting the line profiles in these regions separately, the study calculates the relative RVs for both components. These relative measurements are subsequently combined to determine the total radial velocity. The method's efficacy was validated using a sample of 1,000 LAMOST spectra for which high-precision RVs from the Gaia mission were available. The results indicate that the corrected RVs align closely with Gaia data, exhibiting a mean offset of only 0.002 km/s and a dispersion of 0.02 km/s. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the accuracy of the corrected RVs improves as the line-to-continent ratio (L/C) increases.

This study addresses the reconstruction of an inhomogeneous medium from far-field scattering data obtained via a single fixed source across a spectrum of frequencies. We introduce a deep neural network designed to simultaneously recover the medium's spatial structure and its frequency-dependent properties. The network utilizes equivariant layers to ensure that the reconstructed spatial data maintains the rotational symmetry imposed by the source's location. We demonstrate that the proposed method is capable of accurately solving the inverse scattering problem over a wide range of frequencies.

This study introduces an optimal enhanced degradation-based test framework utilizing a dependent bivariate gamma process to model the degradation of two interconnected components. The proposed model accounts for both the mean and variability of degradation paths, the correlation between components, and their marginal and joint distributions. The study derives the optimal stopping boundaries for both components to maximize the accuracy of estimating their mean degradation, with the optimal strategy determined by minimizing mean squared error. The methodology is illustrated through numerical simulations and a real-world case study involving the testing of two linked components.

We have developed a multiphase transport model to analyze triangular flow ($v_3$) in Au+Au and Cu+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$ GeV. This model incorporates the initial geometry of the collision system, the Landau-Lifshitz hydrodynamic equations, and the Boltzmann transport equation. Our calculations of $v_3$ for Au+Au collisions align well with experimental data from the STAR collaboration. Furthermore, we have examined the $v_3$ dependence on centrality and the mass of the produced particles in Au+Au collisions, as well as the mass dependence in Cu+Au collisions.

Solar wind streams (HSS) and coronal mass ejections (CMEs) are two of the most significant solar wind phenomena, often interacting within the heliosphere. This study investigates the polytropic behavior of the plasma resulting from HSS-CME interactions by analyzing 100 events where HSS encounters CMEs. The analysis utilizes data from the Advanced Composition Explorer (ACE) and Wind spacecraft, covering the period from 1997 to 2019. The findings indicate that the plasma in the interaction region behaves as a polytropic fluid with an index of $\gamma = 1.5$, a characteristic shared by both CMEs and HSS. Furthermore, the shock regions exhibit a polytropic index of $\gamma = 4/3$, consistent with a monatomic ideal gas. These results suggest that the thermodynamic properties of the plasma remain consistent across all three scenarios: isolated HSS, isolated CMEs, and their interaction.

The Random Waypoint (RW) model stands as the most widely utilized approach for simulating mobile entities, including humans and animals. In this framework, each agent selects a random destination and travels at a defined speed, repeating the cycle until the agent's simulated time concludes. This paper introduces a new extension to the RW model that accounts for stochastic traits, specifically focusing on how personality influences an agent's movement. We demonstrate that by assigning a fixed trait value to each agent, the RW model can effectively replicate diverse behavioral patterns, ranging from cautious and slow movement to highly risky and swift navigation. This paper further investigates the interplay between these traits and simulation parameters, such as speed and risk, and analyzes how they affect the statistical distributions of agents' path lengths and dwell times.

This study examines the transverse momentum ($p_T$) distribution of $K^+K^-$ pairs in the effective mass range close to $2m_K$, utilizing data from the ALICE detector at the LHC. The analysis focuses on pairs with $p_T < 1.5$ GeV/$c$ and effective masses between 0.5 and 1.0 GeV/$c^2$. The observed $p_T$ distribution is modeled using a superposition of a Gaussian function and a power-law function. The power-law component is interpreted as arising from mini-jets, whereas the Gaussian component is attributed to thermal emission from a quark-gluon plasma. The results indicate that the fraction of the Gaussian component increases with effective mass, suggesting that the transverse momentum broadening of low-$p_T$ particles is driven by the hadronization process.

The microscopic collective inertial mass, a critical component of the effective Lagrangian used to describe nuclear collective motion, is calculated using the cranking model. This inertial weight is evaluated across various nuclear shapes and densities, with specific attention paid to the influence of nucleonic effective mass. The results indicate that while the effective mass significantly alters inertial behavior, it does so in a manner that is largely independent of the specific nuclear configuration.

This paper outlines the contents of the Representation and Reasoning Corpus, an extensive collection of research papers focused on the representation and reasoning of graph-structured data. The corpus features 139 articles categorized into 13 sub-domains, with each entry providing the title, abstract, citation count, a brief text-based summary, and a link to the full paper. The article further introduces GraphSearch, a Python library designed to facilitate the retrieval and analysis of textual information from research corpora. The discussion concludes by demonstrating GraphSearch's utility through an exploratory analysis of the Representation and Reasoning Corpus.

This study examines conservation laws featuring discontinuous fluxes, focusing on the regularity properties of their weak solutions within the context of the fractional derivative. We demonstrate that such solutions possess $H^s$ regularity for $s < 1$, with the norm $\|s^{\alpha}\|_{H^s}$ scaling as $O(s^{\alpha})$ where $\alpha$ depends on the solution's magnitude; here, the coefficient of the $1/x^{\alpha}$ term in the asymptotic expansion of the flux at the discontinuity dictates this regularity. The result establishes that the regularity of weak solutions is governed by the specific characteristics of the flux near the discontinuity.

This study reports measurements of the branching fractions for $B_{s}^{0} \to D_{s}^{\mp} K^{\pm}$ and $B^{0} \to D_{s}^{-} K^{+}$ decays, utilizing data from proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV recorded by the LHCb detector with an integrated luminosity of 3.0 fb$^{-1}$. The observed branching fractions are determined to be $\mathcal{B}(B_{s}^{0} \to D_{s}^{-} K^{+}) = (1.02 \pm 0.10 \pm 0.05) \times 10^{-4}$ and $\mathcal{B}(B^{0} \to D_{s}^{-} K^{+}) = (1.02 \pm 0.10 \pm 0.05) \times 10^{-4}$, where the first uncertainties are statistical and the second systematic. These values align with predictions derived from the factorization approach.

This study examines a cell-free massive MIMO framework operating in a multicarrier-multicarrier duplex (MC-MDD) configuration, where base units (BUs) employ orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) to mitigate inter-carrier and inter-user interference. The system utilizes a two-tier architecture comprising a central processing unit (CPU) and multiple BUs, with the CPU coordinating the BUs to manage user equipment (UEs). The research evaluates the spectral efficiency (SE) of UEs under various conditions, including different numbers of antennas per BU, varying BU-UE distances, and differing UE counts. Additionally, the study analyzes the impact of inter-cell interference (ICI) and inter-user interference (IUI) on the system's spectral efficiency. The findings indicate that the proposed MC-MDD cell-free massive MIMO architecture delivers superior performance compared to traditional cellular massive MIMO systems.

Differential Privacy (DP) is a rigorous mathematical framework for quantifying privacy risks in data analysis. The Shuffle Model, a recent advancement, offers a privacy assurance stronger than standard DP by leveraging the privacy amplification inherent in shuffling user queries and responses. This paper introduces the concept of "strict accounting" for DP parameters within the Shuffle Model, alongside a corresponding algorithm designed to verify DP bounds derived from any mechanism operating under the Revenue Accounting (RA) framework. We demonstrate that this algorithm is optimal, meaning it achieves the theoretical minimum runtime for any such DP accounting method. Additionally, we present a streamlined implementation of the Shuffle Model that relies on the Revenue Linear Function (RLF) framework, which is compatible with our algorithm. We also supply code for both the algorithm and the model, available on GitHub.

Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) is a prevalent modulation technique in wireless communications, yet it lacks inherent time-domain orthogonality, rendering it vulnerable to inter-carrier interference (ICI) caused by time-varying channels. Orthogonal Time Frequency Multiplexing (OTFS) addresses this by introducing time-domain orthogonality, thereby enhancing performance in such dynamic environments. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the OTFS system, covering its underlying principles, signal processing, and key system parameters. We also explore low-complexity receiver architectures for OTFS, including the Maximum Likelihood (ML) detector, Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP), and a proposed hybrid strategy combining Compressed Sensing (CS) with Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimation. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the MAP-SC-based OTFS receiver delivers superior performance compared to conventional alternatives.

Let $S$ denote a locally compact group and $\mu$ a measure defined on $S$. We define the weighted convolution algebra $\ell^1(S, \mu)$ as the collection of all functions $f: S \to \mathbb{C}$ that are absolutely summable with respect to $\mu$, equipped with the convolution product $(f \ast g)(x) = \int_S f(y)g(y^{-1}x)\,d\mu(y)$. This work investigates the properties of the operator norm on the Banach algebra $\ell^1(S, \mu)$, specifically within the context of its representation on $L^2(X, \nu)$, where $\nu$ is a $\sigma$-finite measure on a $\sigma$-space $X$ acted upon by $S$ via a measure-preserving action.

Laser spot melting is a critical process in additive manufacturing, where the melt pool's shape and behavior dictate the resulting microstructure and material properties. This study employs a 3D numerical model to examine the melting dynamics of a conduction-mode laser spot, specifically focusing on the melt pool's evolution. The model incorporates a thermal-fluid dynamics approach that accounts for the interplay between the liquid metal, molten gas, and solid substrate. The laser beam is mathematically represented as a Gaussian heat source, with the material's thermo-physical properties adjusted based on the temperature. The analysis reveals that the melt pool's geometry is governed by the balance of heat generation, conductive heat loss, and convective heat transfer. The study also investigates the impact of varying laser power and beam radius on the melt pool's characteristics. The findings indicate that the melt pool's depth and width are primarily determined by the ratio of laser power to beam radius, with the pool's shape evolving over time as the melt solidifies. The study concludes that the proposed numerical model accurately captures the essential physics governing laser spot melting and can serve as a valuable tool for optimizing the process parameters in additive manufacturing applications.

This study explores a framework where public transport vehicles (PTVs) serve as platforms for wireless power transfer (WPT) and mobile edge computing (MEC) services. Specifically, the architecture involves a base station (BS) and a power station (PS) supporting two distinct user groups: PTVs and a collection of mobile users (MUs). The system design aims to maximize the total number of successful MEC tasks completed by PTVs while ensuring that the combined energy usage of the PS, the base station, and the PTVs themselves stays within a specific limit. To achieve this, we jointly optimize the allocation of time slots, the positioning of the PS, the distribution of transmit power, and the MUs' computational offloading strategies. The optimization problem is formulated as a mixed-integer non-convex program, which is then resolved using a block coordinate descent method. The results demonstrate that this approach significantly boosts the efficiency of computational task handling for PTVs while maintaining strict energy consumption constraints.

We introduce a novel method for estimating the size of the solution set for Boolean formulas. This approach applies to formulas in Disjunctive Normal Form (DNF) and Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF), as well as formulas with numerical parameters. Our technique relies on a specific "Estimated Degree" metric, a novel concept we define. We demonstrate that the expected number of satisfying assignments for a random formula is bounded by the product of this Estimated Degree and a constant that relies solely on the formula's depth. Consequently, we derive an efficient algorithm to calculate the solution set size for formulas in DNF and CNF, a result that improves upon the previously best-known algorithm by Srinivasan (STOC 1993). Furthermore, we show that the size of the solution set for a formula with parameters is bounded by the product of its Expected Degree, the number of parameters, and a constant that depends only on the formula's depth.

Bistability is a fundamental concept in systems biology, describing the capacity of a system to settle into two distinct stable states in response to external stimuli. This paper introduces a novel method for detecting bistability in continuous dynamical systems by leveraging the Conley index. The proposed approach involves a two-step procedure: first, it identifies a hyperbolic fixed point, and second, it utilizes the Conley index to determine the presence of a limit cycle. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through various illustrative examples, including a classic model of bistability and a system exhibiting both bistability and oscillatory behavior.

This study examines the structure of strange quark stars with aligned spin polarization under finite temperature conditions and strong magnetic fields. The analysis utilizes the MIT bag model, incorporating the Brown-Telegdi precession equation to describe the dynamics of magnetic moments within external fields. The resulting stellar configurations are compared against those of non-magnetized stars. Additionally, we investigate how the magnetic field influences the mass-radius relationship and the maximum mass of these stars.

The integration of audio and visual modalities has become a focal point in multimedia research, offering significant potential for advancing various domains. This paper reviews recent developments in audio-visual correlation learning, focusing on three key areas: sound event detection, lip reading, and audio-visual question answering. We examine both the application domains and their respective methodologies, while also highlighting persistent challenges and promising future directions.

The Linear Ordering Problem (LOP) is a well-known issue in combinatorial optimization that seeks to identify a linear arrangement of items to maximize a specific objective function. This objective is typically defined as the sum of weights of edges oriented from a higher item to a lower item. While LOP is NP-hard, it is frequently utilized as a proxy for the more complex Feedback Arc Set (FAS) problem, which targets minimizing the weight of edges oriented in the "wrong" direction. This paper investigates the probabilistic characteristics of solutions to the Linear Ordering Problem, demonstrating that under a uniform random weight distribution, the optimal linear ordering aligns with a specific stochastic property.

We have examined the phase-fluctuation phenomena in NbN superconducting nanofilms, which exhibit a granular structure. By analyzing the temperature dependence of the upper critical field ($H_{c2}$) near the superconductor-insulator transition, we identified a crossover from a regime dominated by phase fluctuations to one governed by quantum fluctuations. Furthermore, we observed that the superconductor-insulator critical temperature ($T_{cI}$) increases with film thickness, a trend attributed to the emergence of a phase-fluctuation contribution to $T_{cI}$ in these granular films.

This paper introduces Temporal Traversal Traversal Trail Queries (T-TRQs), a new class of temporal graph query designed to identify trails—non-repetitive walks that may revisit vertices—based on time-constrained edge conditions. T-TRQs are defined by a Temporal Regular Expression (TRE) that specifies the required sequence of edges. We present an efficient algorithm capable of answering T-TRQs in time complexity $O(m + n + |\mathcal{T}|)$, where $m$ represents the number of edges, $n$ the number of vertices, and $|\mathcal{T}|$ denotes the count of matching trails. Furthermore, we developed a practical system named T-TRQ-Searcher to evaluate T-TRQs on real-world temporal datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed system effectively and efficiently resolves T-TRQs on these datasets.

This study introduces a novel method for decelerating free radicals using concurrent operation within a lithium atom-based Zeeman decelerator. The proposed technique enables the generation of a cold, trapped, and highly pure sample of polyatomic free radicals. By utilizing the specific spin dynamics of these radicals, the approach allows for the selective accumulation of decelerated particles within a trap. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves a trapping efficiency exceeding 90% for methyl free radicals. Furthermore, the concurrent deceleration mechanism facilitates the production of polyatomic free radicals at temperatures below 100 mK, thereby opening new avenues for quantum investigations into such polyatomic systems.

The Swift satellite's Burst Alert System (BAT) and Gamma-Ray Burst Monitor (GBM) are designed to detect and localize gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) and other transient events. The BAT instrument is capable of identifying a wide range of transients, including supernovae, while the GBM is sensitive to both long-duration and short-duration gamma-ray bursts. The software responsible for identifying and classifying these events is the Swift-XRT Point Source catalogue (XSPEC), which is a publicly available, open-source tool. The XSPEC code is written in Python and uses the Swift-XTE library to process the data from the Swift-XTE instrument. We investigate the spin-1/2 XY model defined by the Hamiltonian $H = J_1 \sum_{\langle ij\rangle} S_i^z S_j^z + J_2 \sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle} S_i^z S_j^z + \sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle} (S_i^+ S_j^- + h.c.) + h \sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle} S_i^z$, where $h$ represents an external magnetic field. By employing the infinite projected entangled pair state (iPEPS) method, we determine the ground state phase diagram of the system. Our results indicate that the plaquette valence bond phase emerges at specific regions of the parameter space, particularly when the magnetic field is applied.

This study introduces a decomposition framework for bilateral exchange flows grounded in a three-dimensional panel data model. The resulting methodology partitions these flows into distinct components: specific bilateral pairs, broader regional patterns, attributes of exporting and importing nations, and a residual term. We apply this approach to analyze global trade data spanning 1995 to 2019. The analysis reveals that roughly 60% of the flow variations are driven by individual exporting and importing country characteristics, with an additional 15% attributable to regional patterns. The residual component, which captures the specific mix of regional, national, and other factors, is further divided into two parts: a trend component and a random component. The trend component, representing long-term dynamics, accounts for approximately 40% of the total variation, while the random component represents short-term fluctuations.

This study examines the noncommutative modifications of $U(1)$ gauge theory in four dimensions, specifically focusing on the non-Abelian deformation of the $U(1)$ field strength. We establish the existence of consistent extensions involving higher derivatives and non-locality, which are compatible with Lorentz symmetry. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the resulting deformed field equations can be systematically derived using the $\mathcal{L}_{\infty}$ bootstrap framework.

Time perception is the cognitive process of gauging the passage of time. This study introduces a wearable-based approach to continuously assess time perception duration, which serves as an indicator of mental health. The methodology involves collecting time perception data from 20 participants over a 14-day period using smartwatches. The system automatically prompts users to complete time-estimation tasks, asking them to report how long a specific interval felt. The resulting dataset is then analyzed to derive the time perception duration. Results indicate that the proposed system effectively and unobtrusively monitors time perception duration in real-world settings.

This paper examines the consistency between US law and fairness concepts within machine learning. We begin by outlining the legal framework governing fairness in ML algorithms, followed by a review of existing fairness definitions and their alignment with US statutes. We identify discrepancies in legal compliance across various definitions and introduce new formulations that better adhere to US law. Ultimately, we argue that achieving legal compliance in fairness definitions is a viable objective.

This study introduces a theoretical model for detecting neutrino pair discharge (PPD) via the magnetization of trivalent lanthanide ions. The proposed mechanism relies on the magnetic anisotropy of these ions, which exhibits a directional dependence on the applied magnetic field. Theoretically, this approach offers a significant advantage over existing PPD detection methods by eliminating the need for ultra-low background conditions.

This study investigates the binding energies of single and double strange hypernuclei with mass numbers up to $A=8$ using an efficient field theory framework. The analysis employs a chiral effective Lagrangian for nucleon-nucleon and $\Lambda$-nucleon interactions alongside a phenomenological $\Sigma N$ interaction. The model parameters are fitted to established ground-state binding energies of light hypernuclei, specifically $\Lambda$-nuclei, $\Xi$-nuclei, and $\Sigma$-nuclei. The calculated binding energies are then benchmarked against recent experimental data.

This paper introduces MetaPriv, a browser extension designed to help users on social media platforms make informed choices regarding their privacy. MetaPriv operates by providing actionable privacy guidance based on the specific context of the user's profile. It does this by analyzing profile settings and calculating the privacy risk associated with individual actions before they occur. By calculating these risks in real-time, MetaPriv empowers users to adjust their behavior proactively to ensure their personal information remains protected.

This paper investigates the coalescent mechanism within the population dynamics of a branching process evolving under a changing environment, specifically one driven by the linear-fractional branching mechanism. We demonstrate that the coalescent process, defined as the collection of ancestral line locations, behaves asymptotically like a specific point process derived from the linear-fractional mechanism, with appropriate scaling applied.

This study examines the Hamiltonian chain (HC) model on $\mathbb{Z}^d$, where the interaction between neighboring spins $s$ and $s'$ is defined by $J(s,s') = \frac{1}{s(s'+1)}$. Furthermore, we establish the existence of an uncountable collection of non-translation-invariant Gibbs measures. Finally, we analyze the phase diagram of this HC model.

By employing the all-order Breit interaction alongside a relativistic effective core potential, the approach achieves a theoretical precision of approximately 100 MHz, which is sufficiently accurate to detect nuclear recoil effects in the isotope shifts of indium.

A previously established necessary condition for 0.15 existence fails to be sufficient. This paper introduces a fundamental criterion that is both necessary and sufficient for the existence of such transversals. The proof of this condition relies on the Axiom of Choice.

The proliferation of mobile devices with diverse screen sizes and resolutions has made video transcoding essential for delivering optimized content tailored to specific device capabilities. This study introduces a transcoding framework designed to generate high-quality, device-specific video streams by leveraging cloud-based services. The system utilizes Amazon EC2 instances to host video transcoding jobs, employing the Amazon Elastic Transcode service to reconfigure video parameters for target devices. A primary challenge in this architecture is the efficient assignment of video jobs to appropriate transcoding instances. To address this, we developed a performance model that evaluates the benefits of parallel transcoding workflows. The study also assesses the system's scalability by analyzing how the number of concurrent video jobs impacts overall performance.

This study examines the impact of cycle counts on the performance of the classic 2-SAT algorithm developed by Aspvall, Tarjan, and Goldschlag. We demonstrate that a specific variant of the algorithm, which terminates immediately upon finding a contradiction, achieves optimal average-case complexity by running in linear time on average. This behavior relies on the algorithm's ability to skip cycles that contain only a limited number of literals.

This paper demonstrates that the ground state of the energy ultracritical Gross--Pitaevskii equation corresponds to a function with zero Morse index. Furthermore, we establish that any positive solution of the associated stationary equation, characterized by a negative Morse index, is radially symmetric about the origin. These findings advance the understanding of the ultracritical regime, which is of particular interest in the study of energy-critical nonlinear Schrödinger equations.

This study introduces a robust framework for Type I error control in the assessment of automated design optimization, addressing the complexities of evaluating automated systems where the decision to select a design is inherently tied to the statistical testing methodology. Unlike traditional approaches that treat the selection rule as fixed, our perspective accounts for the inherent variability in the testing procedure. We provide a formal definition of error control in this automated context and introduce a novel class of tests capable of maintaining error rates at or below a specified level. These methods are applicable to both parametric and nonparametric testing scenarios. We demonstrate the utility of our framework through two practical examples: a parametric test for mean differences and a nonparametric test based on the Siegel-Tukey statistic. Simulation results confirm that our method successfully preserves Type I error rates while delivering reliable statistical power.

We introduce Distributed Hybrid Rendering (DHR), a framework designed to deliver immersive virtual experiences by leveraging distributed graphics processing. This architecture enables the transmission of virtual reality (VR) content to remote clients while maintaining low latency and high fidelity. DHR achieves this through a hybrid strategy that combines geometry sharing, specifically utilizing a distributed mesh where geometry is rendered centrally and only geometry data is sent to distributed nodes, alongside foveated rendering that optimizes quality based on the user's gaze. This approach significantly reduces the bandwidth required for high-quality VR delivery. We evaluated the DHR framework using a distributed cluster equipped with NVIDIA DGX-1 servers and a high-performance workstation featuring an NVIDIA Titan Xp GPU, testing it with the VR game *Superhot VR*. Our results demonstrate that the system achieves up to 100 fps at a resolution of 1800 x 1800 pixels per eye with a 10 ms end-to-end end-to-end latency, a performance level previously unattainable on a single workstation.

This study investigates the impact of annotation and alignment accuracy on the performance of music information retrieval (MIR) systems analyzing complex orchestral works. We conducted a systematic evaluation involving 10 MIR benchmarks, each comprising 100 system outputs, with annotations and alignments perturbed by errors ranging from 1 to 5 seconds. Results indicate that performance degradation varies significantly across different tasks, with pitch detection and chord recognition exhibiting high sensitivity to misalignments, whereas polyphonic source separation and music synthesis proved relatively robust. We also examined the impact of annotation errors, finding that pitch detection and polyphonic separation are more vulnerable to such inaccuracies than other tasks. Ultimately, the findings suggest that when comparing MIR systems, the intrinsic difficulty of the specific task must be accounted for, as the precision requirements for annotations and alignments differ substantially depending on the task.

The Full-Duplex (FD) radio, capable of transmitting and receiving data simultaneously on the same frequency, offers a significant advantage over traditional half-duplex (FDxR) systems by doubling the spectral efficiency. However, the ability to transmit and receive concurrently introduces substantial self-interference (SI), which can saturate the receiver and compromise communication reliability. To address this, researchers have developed various SI suppression strategies, including analog and digital beamforming, as well as analog and digital self-interference cancellation (SIxC). This paper presents an overview of these techniques, specifically analyzing analog and digital SIxC methods alongside multibeamforming approaches. The study evaluates the effectiveness of these methods in achieving the necessary SI suppression for practical FD implementation. Furthermore, it examines the advantages and challenges associated with deploying multiantenna FD systems.

Collapsing liquid droplets are a common occurrence in nature, with their infolding dynamics playing a critical role in biological processes such as embryogenesis. This study investigates the buckling and folding mechanisms during droplet consolidation using high-resolution imaging and quantitative analysis. We demonstrate that the onset of buckling is governed by the balance between surface tension and bending rigidity, with the bending rigidity being determined by the thickness of the coalesced droplet skin. The critical thickness required to initiate buckling is found to be a function of the capillary number, which characterizes the drainage phase. Furthermore, we observe that the rate of infolding depends on both the capillary number and the volume of the droplet.

This technique is based on the fact that the disk's midplane density profile follows a power law, $H(r) \propto r^{\alpha}$, where $r$ represents the radial distance. The observed flux from these disks is governed by the radial distribution of the incident stellar radiation field, which in turn relies on the disk's optical depth. We demonstrate that the slope of the UV emission profile, defined as $q = d\log(F_{\rm UV}/F_{\rm UV,1}) / d\log(r/r_1)$, is directly linked to the power-law exponent of the density profile through the relation $q = 1 - \alpha$. By utilizing the well-established relationship between UV flux and disk mass, $F_{\rm UV} \propto M_{\rm disk}$, we can derive the disk mass from the measured flux. Consequently, this approach enables the determination of the disk mass and the power-law exponent $\alpha$ for any disk exhibiting detectable UV emission. This paper introduces a new fingerprint-based millimeter-wave (mmWave) localization framework that leverages reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS). The system utilizes RIS-enhanced channels to generate fingerprints for creating a localization map, which is then applied to estimate the user equipment's (UE) position. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses existing approaches, such as those relying solely on line-of-sight (LoS) or non-line-of-sight (NLoS) channels, by achieving a 30% reduction in root mean square error (RMSE) when using LoS channels and a 40% reduction when using NLoS channels.

We investigate the generation of twisted particles within constant magnetic fields using classical mechanics, focusing on the influence of the initial velocity vector's orientation relative to the field. Our findings indicate that a non-zero orbital angular momentum can emerge even when particles originate from an isotropic distribution, provided their initial velocities are not collinear with the magnetic field. Consequently, this orbital momentum induces a magnetic moment, causing the twisted particles to rotate around the field lines; notably, the rotation frequency is independent of the particle's mass.

The surge in electric vehicle (EV) adoption is driving a significant increase in demand for charging infrastructure. This growth presents a dual challenge: managing the power grid's capacity and optimizing the charging network's economic viability. This study addresses these issues by examining the location of charging stations, pricing strategies, and market architectures. We introduce a new framework that integrates location and pricing decisions into a unified model, which is then applied to design a market mechanism facilitating charging access. We demonstrate that this new framework and associated market design can alleviate congestion, enhance the operational efficiency of charging stations, and improve economic outcomes for all stakeholders.

Tie-breaker experiments are designed to resolve ties that occur in A/B testing. In these studies, when participants encounter equal perceived value between two options, their choices are recorded, and the analysis focuses exclusively on this subset. The primary goal is to derive the purest possible estimate of relative preference strength. We demonstrate that existing literature on these designs is grounded in flawed assumptions regarding the data-generating process. Consequently, we offer a rigorous mathematical framework for analyzing tie-breaker experiments, establishing that current methods are suboptimal. Our findings also reveal that, in certain scenarios, simply discarding tied-out choices yields a superior estimator compared to retaining them.

We have derived all possible three-point correlation functions of super-spinor currents within ${\mathcal N}=1$ superconformal theories, utilizing the operator product expansion (OPE) of these currents. Our results are consistent with the ${\mathcal N}=1$ superconformal Ward identities, which we also demonstrate are equivalent to the constraints imposed by the three OPEs of the super-spinor currents. Furthermore, we confirm that the three-point functions can be constructed using ${\mathcal N}=1$ superconformal three-point functions of scalar supermultiplets by incorporating appropriate super-spinor indices.

Children possess an innate drive to understand how the world functions, a trait that can be harnessed to demystify computer architecture. While various educational programs have attempted to make machine instructions accessible to young learners, the degree to which they succeed remains uncertain. This study examines the extent of children's natural curiosity regarding machine instructions and their grasp of these concepts through three distinct experiments. The first experiment reveals that children are naturally fascinated by machine instructions. The second experiment demonstrates that they can acquire knowledge about these instructions via short, story-based lessons. The third experiment indicates that children can achieve a solid comprehension of machine instructions, evidenced by their ability to execute them on a Raspberry Pi. Collectively, these findings offer compelling evidence for the potential of a new pedagogical strategy: teaching machine instructions to children through brief narrative lessons.

Although artificial intelligence has achieved significant milestones, it has not yet matched human capabilities in domains like language fluency, driving, or common sense reasoning. A primary reason for this shortfall is the absence of enduring reinforcement learning (RL) systems. This paper reviews recent progress in enduring RL, explores the challenges that remain, and proposes potential pathways for future research.

We present an on-chip integrated photonic chip featuring a reconfigurable circuit designed to convert quantum information across various degrees of freedom (DOFs). Utilizing a hybrid approach that combines a spatial light modulator with the chip, we demonstrate the coherent transformation of quantum states between different DOFs, specifically converting spatial-mode entangled photons into polarization-encoded qubit pairs. This architecture enables the realization of a quantum switch that operates on both spatial-mode and polarization-encoded quantum inputs.

The study investigates quantum conduction in DNA strands containing mispairs using the tight-binding model, specifically examining how the degree of quantum conductance varies with the location of mispairs. Results indicate that quantum conductive levels are notably higher in regions where mispairs are located closer to the DNA ends. These findings are attributed to the unique characteristics of electronic wave functions near the DNA boundaries.

Point cloud registration is a critical task in computer vision and graphics, yet it remains difficult due to the presence of outliers and the need for computational efficiency. This paper introduces an efficient, robust method for registering point sets that utilizes a two-stage strategy. First, a clustering-based approach registers local clusters of points, followed by a global registration step that aggregates these results. The local clustering method draws inspiration from K-means but adapts the process to handle registration directly. Specifically, it employs a modified K-medians algorithm to partition points into clusters and then registers each group using a closed-form solution. This differs from traditional K-means, which clusters based on feature similarity. By integrating this robust variant of K-means with the registration pipeline, the proposed approach achieves greater resilience to outliers. Experimental results demonstrate that this method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in both accuracy and speed.

We report on the magnetic structure of Tb$_3$Ru$_7$O$_{12}$, a compound featuring alternating-bond spin-3/2 Ru chains situated within a nonuniform internal magnetic field generated by tetragonal Tb$^{3+}$ ions. Our findings reveal a partially disordered state characterized by a combination of ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic spin correlations, which develops at $T_N = 10.5$ K. This state is attributed to the interplay between the nonuniform internal field and the intrinsic properties of spin-3/2 systems.

This study examines minimax problems with constraint conditions, classified as DC (difference of convex) constrained mathematical programming tasks. By employing DC representations for both the objective function and constraints, we establish new necessary optimality conditions. These findings are then leveraged to define new optimality criteria for DC constrained minimax problems. The section concludes by presenting several illustrative examples to validate the efficacy of these derived results.

The approach utilizes a differentiable deconvolution method that integrates directly with a perfusion model, optimizing both components jointly. The resulting system, termed DiffDeconPerk, demonstrates superior performance compared to conventional serial perfusion analysis techniques.

We present the first complete next-to-next-to-next-to-leading order (N$^3$LO) QCD prediction for the jet-veto (zero-jettiness) cross-section in Drell-Yan production at the LHC. For a finite group $G$, the *unit power graph* $\mathcal{P}(G)$ is defined as a graph with vertex set $G^*$, comprising all elements of order greater than one, where two vertices are connected by an edge if one is a power of the other. This paper investigates the properties of $\mathcal{P}(G)$, specifically determining precisely when $\mathcal{P}(G)$ is chordal, identifying the conditions under which it forms a complete graph, and examining situations where it is bipartite.

This study addresses the challenge of isolating a specific source amidst a noisy backdrop. We introduce a method designed to enhance the quality of a specific source by first training a deep neural network to identify the target's environment and then utilizing this information to perform source separation. We demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves superior separation performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

We introduce a framework for identifying consistency in quantum states relative to general measurements. Specifically, we demonstrate that the quantum state consistency problem can be resolved in the polynomial hierarchy (PH) by establishing a connection to the problem of consistent quantum measurement.

We report the discovery of Type C Quasi-Periodic Oscillations (CQPOs) in the transient X-ray binary H 1743--322, observed during three separate outbursts in 2016 and 2017. These CQPOs exhibit a broad frequency range of 1.0--10.0 Hz, with a mean value of 3.5 Hz, and display a prominent "bump" structure in their power spectra. This feature is interpreted as the presence of an accretion structure, likely a hot accretion flow, situated between the black hole and the accretion disk. Our analysis reveals that the mean frequency of this bump structure remains nearly constant across all three outbursts, whereas the widths of the bumps vary significantly. We propose that these variations in width reflect changes in the accretion structure's size, which in turn are driven by fluctuations in the mass accretion rate.

Open-source software is essential for the advancement of open governments, as it empowers the public to access and utilize government services more effectively. This paper outlines the development of an open-source Question Answering (QA) system designed to enhance e-governance. This QA platform functions as a search engine capable of delivering precise answers to user queries. We detail the underlying infrastructure, including the data collection methods, data preprocessing techniques, and the specific QA model employed. Furthermore, we present a range of questions submitted by users to demonstrate the platform's practical application.

This paper investigates this discrepancy using the EAGLE cosmological hydrodynamical simulation suite. We analyze the radial distribution of baryons in the simulation, revealing that the EAGLE model successfully reproduces the observed baryon fraction in the local universe. We find that approximately 10% of baryons are located within the Milky Way's virial radius, 20% reside in the warm-hot intergalactic medium (WHIM) within the same radius, and 70% are found in the WHIM outside this radius. A "leftmost $k$"-divider of a string $S$ refers to the shortest prefix $P$ of $S$ such that the longest common suffix of $P$ and $P$ reversed is at least $k$. This paper establishes that all leftmost $k$-dividers of a string $S$ can be identified in linear time, $\mathcal{O}(|S|)$, utilizing a suffix automaton. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, given a string $S$ and a length bound $k$, it is possible to enumerate every leftmost $k$-divider in output-sensitive time, defined as $\mathcal{O}(|S| + n \log n)$, where $n$ represents the count of such dividers.

We investigate the stellar velocity dispersion ($\sigma$) and central surface brightness of galaxies within the $0.6 < z < 1.2$ redshift range, utilizing a sample of 100 post-starburst (PSB) and 100 Balmer-strong (BS) galaxies from the Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS). Our analysis reveals that PSB galaxies exhibit a $\sigma$ distribution peaking at 100 km/s, whereas BS galaxies peak at 180 km/s. The BS population displays a broader $\sigma$ distribution, extending up to 250 km/s, compared to the PSB population, which is confined below 150 km/s. We identify two distinct subpopulations within the BS group: a high-$\sigma$ component ($>180$ km/s) and a low-$\sigma$ component ($<180$ km/s). The high-$\sigma$ BSs are characterized by high mass, high surface brightness, and high star formation rates (SFRs), while the low-$\sigma$ BSs are low mass, low surface brightness, and low SFR. We also detect a low-$\sigma$ subpopulation in the PSB group, which is less massive and has lower surface brightness than the high-$\sigma$ PSB component. Reconfigurable Wireless Networks (RWNs) offer a promising solution for meeting the stringent demands of emerging applications, such as autonomous driving and remote surgery. However, the dynamic nature of RWNs, characterized by fluctuating channel conditions and shifting traffic loads, complicates the task of allocating limited resources effectively. To address this, we introduce PCQL, a novel QoS-aware scheduler that leverages the synergy between deep reinforcement learning (DRL) and deep learning. PCQL employs a performer-critic architecture to simultaneously optimize both the policy and the value function, thereby enhancing the accuracy of reward estimation. Furthermore, the algorithm incorporates a multi-agent mechanism to manage the diverse requirements of multiple users. Simulation results demonstrate that PCQL outperforms existing scheduling methods in terms of throughput, fairness, and computational efficiency.

This study introduces a new approach to assess the precision of machine translation (MT) outputs specifically designed to aid post-editors. By utilizing a set of 1,000 human-translated English sentences alongside 1,000 corresponding MT sentences, we developed a model capable of predicting the percentage of words that will require editing. This method achieves a mean absolute error of 1.9% on an independent test set, with an accuracy of 90% for identifying cases where word-level correction is unnecessary. Furthermore, we demonstrate that MT systems trained on domain-specific corpora yield higher prediction accuracy than those trained on general data.

This study investigates the Kerr--de Sitter spacetime, specifically focusing on black holes within a universe containing a non-negligible cosmological constant. We demonstrate that this constant can be uniquely determined from the silhouettes of such black holes, provided the silhouette is observed from a fixed radial distance. Furthermore, we show that this unique determination holds true even when the silhouette is viewed from infinity.

This work presents a novel, more robust framework for solving the relativistic hydrodynamic equations in two-dimensional Cartesian coordinates. The primary advancement involves expressing the four-velocity components using the square root of the sum of three terms, ensuring that the resulting velocity remains subluminal. This approach guarantees that the velocity constraints are inherently satisfied, eliminating the need for additional enforcement. The method is validated by applying it to two-dimensional simulations of the Richtmyer–Schaumann instability and a cylindrical configuration representing a relativistic fireball generated in heavy-ion collisions. These simulations demonstrate that the proposed formulation yields results consistent with established solutions.

Furthermore, the study investigates their connection to the Riesz product and investigates their behavior under the three symmetry operations that preserve the Sierpiński gasket.

This study introduces a novel framework for creating questions that are specifically tailored to a given image. By utilizing an image-text joint model, the system generates a diverse range of questions across different categories, including those focused on object attributes, relationships, and reasoning. The model employs a generator equipped with image-conditioning to produce answers alongside queries, utilizing specialized text decoders to assess the relevance of generated questions to their corresponding images. The proposed approach is evaluated through both quantitative metrics and qualitative human assessments, demonstrating its effectiveness in producing image-specific questions.

The "cusp-core" discrepancy represents a significant mismatch between the density profiles of dark matter halos observed in simulations versus those detected in actual galaxies. This paper examines the mechanism by which a supernova-driven (SN-driven) feedback process transforms dark matter halos from a central cusp profile to a flat, core-like structure. We find that this transformation occurs when the ratio of the SN-driven feedback energy to the gravitational potential energy of the dark matter exceeds a critical threshold. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the ratio of the SN-driven wind mass outflow to the dark matter inflow is directly proportional to this ratio of energies. Consequently, the process of converting a cusp into a core can be effectively described by the mass outflow ratio of the SN-driven wind relative to the dark matter accretion.

This paper presents two novel advanced elimination techniques tailored for the Boolean satisfiability problem. The first method, termed "dual unit propagation," is a sophisticated strategy that generalizes standard unit propagation to eliminate a broader range of literals. The second method, called "extended rule-based reduction," extends conventional rule-based elimination to support specific scenarios involving dual implicability. Our analysis demonstrates that both novel methods are strictly more powerful than their traditional counterparts.

This study examines the dynamics of replicator equations derived from finite games where the payoff matrix $A$ is related to itself via a similarity transformation $A = cB$ ($c > 0$). We demonstrate that the resulting dynamical system preserves both the sum of absolute row sums and the sum of absolute column sums of $A$. Leveraging these properties, we establish the stability of the system's stationary points and analyze the behavior of its solutions. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence between the stability of stationary points in the replicator equation and the stability of fixed points in the original game. Finally, we apply these findings to a specific class of evolutionary games.

This study establishes the asymptotic typicality of multivariate random forest estimators, which are known to converge in probability almost surely to their target regression function. Building upon this limiting behavior, we derive a central limit theorem (CLT) for these forests, yielding an asymptotic estimator that is Gaussian. Our proof relies on two key components: first, an adaptation of the original asymptotic typicality concept to smooth functionals, and second, a new CLT for multivariate nearest neighbor estimators. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the asymptotic variance of the random forest estimator is strictly lower than that of standard kernel estimators, thereby confirming the superior efficiency of forests in the asymptotic regime. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings through simulations and an application to real-world data.

This study introduces a communication-restricted alternating direction method of multipliers (CR-ADMM) approach to address electric vehicle (EV) charging within unbalanced distribution grids. The CR-ADMM algorithm is designed to minimize total electricity costs while ensuring balanced load distribution and avoiding voltage violations, all while requiring minimal data exchange between the distribution system operator (DSO) and local agents. The method operates by distributing the problem into three sub-problems: one managed by the DSO and two managed by local agents. The DSO's component utilizes a relaxed version of the three-phase power flow model to ensure feasible solutions, whereas the local agents employ a quadratic approximation of local cost functions to generate easily solvable sub-problems. The CR-ADMM framework is proven to converge to a solution that satisfies the original problem's Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions. Furthermore, the algorithm's ability to operate under limited communication constraints is a key feature. Simulation results demonstrate that the CR-ADMM algorithm successfully reduces operational costs and achieves balanced loading while maintaining compliance with voltage limits.

Metabolic reconstruction is a critical component of computational systems biology, serving as a foundational step for analyzing metabolic networks and cellular pathways. Although numerous computational methods have been developed to reconstruct bacterial metabolism, the majority of these approaches depend on manually curating metabolic reactions and genes, a process that is laborious and prone to human error. Consequently, there is a pressing need for automated, scalable, and accurate reconstruction methods. This study introduces a novel, automated framework for reconstructing bacterial metabolism. By leveraging the extensive genomic and metabolic databases available, our approach integrates various bioinformatics tools to extract and link genomic and metabolic data, thereby generating metabolism-aware genome-scale models. We successfully applied this method to reconstruct metabolic models for 100 bacterial species. Our results demonstrate that the generated models are both comprehensive and precise, effectively capturing the metabolic pathways of the target organisms.

The widespread integration of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) in building systems has enabled the creation of intelligent structures capable of monitoring and managing their own operations. A primary advantage of smart buildings is their ability to enhance energy efficiency by utilizing real-time data to optimize subsystem performance. This study focuses on the ventilation component of a building's infrastructure, which is critical for indoor air quality and significantly impacts energy consumption. By examining the specific role of ventilation within a smart building framework, we propose a model that leverages data-driven techniques to improve its operational efficiency. This approach involves developing a data preprocessing workflow to generate features that capture the ventilation system's behavior and constructing a machine learning model to forecast energy usage. The model's performance was evaluated using a dataset from a real-world smart building, with results demonstrating that the proposed method achieves high accuracy in predicting energy consumption.
